content: Greater burdock, also known as edible burdock or Lappa burdock, is a biennial plant belonging to the Arctium genus within the Asteraceae family. It is cultivated in gardens primarily for its root, which is used as a vegetable. Greater burdock is a tall plant, capable of growing up to 2 meters in height. Its leaves are large, alternate, and heart-shaped, with long petioles. The underside of the leaves is covered in fine hairs, giving it a pubescent texture. The plant produces purple flowers that are grouped into spherical clusters called capitula, which appear during mid-summer. These capitula are surrounded by an involucre composed of numerous bracts. Each bract curves into a hook-like shape, enabling the capitula to attach to the fur of animals and be dispersed over long distances. The fruits of the plant are achenes, which are elongated, compressed, and have short pappuses. The plant's taproot is fleshy and can grow up to 1 meter in length. Greater burdock is native to temperate regions of the Old World, ranging from Scandinavia to the Mediterranean, and extending from the British Isles through Russia, the Middle East, China, and Japan, including parts of India. It has become naturalized in many regions worldwide and is commonly found in disturbed areas, particularly in nitrogen-rich soils. In Japan, it is widely cultivated and has even lent its name to a specific construction technique known as burdock piling. The plant thrives in well-drained, humus-rich soil that has been freshly worked. It requires full sunlight for optimal growth and responds strongly to nitrogen-based fertilizers. Propagation is typically achieved by directly sowing seeds in mid-summer. The roots are harvested three to four months after sowing, continuing until late autumn, at which point the roots become too fibrous for use. In traditional medicine, dried greater burdock is regarded by folk herbalists as a diuretic, a diaphoretic (promoting sweating), and a blood purifier. The seeds of greater burdock are also used in traditional Chinese medicine, where they are referred to as niupangzi.
